claims.text: The balance between configurational entropy, atomic-size mismatch, and surface-energy disparities governs retention of a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles have a homogeneous solid-solution crystalline phase.
Atomic-level mixing uniformity mediates resistance to phase separation.
Grain-boundary and surface energies mediate resistance to phase separation.
At moderate temperatures, high configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous phase.
Atomic-size and surface-energy differences impose free-energy penalties on the homogeneous phase.
Enhanced atomic mobility can cause diffusion-driven local segregation or phase nucleation.
Well-mixed nanoparticles will retain structural and chemical stability up to a critical temperature.
Nanoparticles with reduced mixing uniformity will begin phase separation at a lower temperature than well-mixed nanoparticles.
Phase separation will be accompanied by degradation of catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
At 473 K, the nanoparticles have a uniform single-phase solid solution with even elemental distribution.
At 473 K, the nanoparticles have stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Inert or reducing atmospheres minimize oxidation during operation and annealing.
Oxidizing environments or extrinsic impurities may alter the proposed thermodynamic balance.
The phase-separation threshold depends on the particular metal combination and processing details.
XRD peak splitting or the appearance of new diffraction peaks can indicate phase separation.

contradictions.description: The defined initial state and 473 K baseline describe homogeneous, evenly distributed nanoparticles, whereas one comparison batch is deliberately initialized with inhomogeneity. The baseline is therefore not consistently defined for both experimental groups.
